headline: **Role** is the job a player actually has on his own team right now, worked out from his last three games rather than from where he was drafted. **Flags** after it are things he is doing unusually well for that job. A flag marked *(1 game)* happened once; anything else held across the window.

groups.title: Roles — the job he has
groups.lede: One per player. Worked out from his last three games, not from where he was drafted, so it changes during the season when his usage does.

rows.what it means: His team's number one receiver — he gets thrown at more than any other wideout on the roster.
rows.why it matters: The safest kind of receiver to start. Volume holds up even in bad games.

rows.what it means: The second receiver on his team.
rows.why it matters: Usually startable, but he needs the offence to move the ball to pay off.

rows.what it means: The third receiver, and on the field for at least half his team's plays.
rows.why it matters: A flex play in good matchups. One injury ahead of him changes everything.

rows.what it means: Fourth or lower in the receiver pecking order, or barely on the field.
rows.why it matters: Not startable as things stand. Worth watching only if his role grows.

rows.what it means: His team's starting tight end, and one they actually throw to.
rows.why it matters: The only kind of tight end worth a lineup spot most weeks.

rows.what it means: His team's starting tight end, but he is out there to block — the passes rarely come his way.
rows.why it matters: Plays a lot and scores nothing. Snap counts will flatter him.

rows.what it means: A second-string tight end, behind the starter in both playing time and targets.
rows.why it matters: Only matters if the starter gets hurt.

rows.what it means: He gets most of his team's carries — more than half of them.
rows.why it matters: The workhorse. Volume alone makes him startable.

rows.what it means: He splits the carries with another back, taking roughly a third to a half of them.
rows.why it matters: Touchdown-dependent. A good week needs the ball near the goal line.

rows.what it means: He does not get many carries, but he is the back they throw to — often the one on the field on third down.
rows.why it matters: Worth more in this league than in most, because catches score half a point each.

rows.what it means: A reserve back with no regular role.
rows.why it matters: A handcuff at best. He needs an injury ahead of him.

rows.what it means: His team's starting quarterback.
rows.why it matters: Only starters are worth rostering at quarterback.

rows.what it means: A backup quarterback — he is not starting unless something happens to the man ahead of him.
rows.why it matters: Nothing to do here unless the starter goes down.

groups.title: Flags — what he is doing well
groups.lede: A player can carry several. These are measured against others in the SAME role, so a third receiver is judged against other third receivers.

rows.what it means: He is doing the job of the man above him — a third receiver producing like a second, or a committee back running like the lead.
rows.why it matters: The strongest buy signal here. Offences tend to notice this before fantasy managers do.

rows.what it means: He is producing less than the man BELOW him on the depth chart.
rows.why it matters: His job is at risk. Sell or drop before the snap count catches up.

rows.what it means: A big share of his team's throws go his way — far more than is normal for his spot in the pecking order.
rows.why it matters: Targets are the most repeatable thing a receiver does. This is the flag that survives a quiet week.

rows.what it means: He is the one they throw deep to, not just the one they throw often to.
rows.why it matters: Big-play upside, and more week-to-week swing. Boom or bust.

rows.what it means: He rarely leaves the field.
rows.why it matters: Playing time is the floor under everything else. It usually comes before the production does.

rows.what it means: He is taking the clear majority of his team's running plays.
rows.why it matters: Workload like this survives a bad game. Coaches do not bench it.

rows.what it means: He is the one getting the ball inside the ten-yard line.
rows.why it matters: This is where touchdowns come from, and touchdowns are six points.

rows.what it means: He is the one who would take over if the starter ahead of him got hurt.
rows.why it matters: Worth a bench spot even while he does nothing, and worth more if you already own the starter.

rows.what it means: When he is thrown to, it tends to produce a first down.
rows.why it matters: Chain-movers keep drives alive, so offences keep going back to them.

groups.title: How long it has held
groups.lede: The difference between a pattern and a good afternoon.

rows.what it means: It happened in one game only, not across the three being looked at.
rows.why it matters: Could be the start of something, could be a good matchup. Not proof of anything yet.

rows.what it means: It has held for at least two of his last three games.
rows.why it matters: A pattern, not an afternoon.

groups.title: Vegas — what the betting market says
groups.lede: **Vegas pts** is this week's sportsbook player props scored in half-PPR. One thing worth knowing: a posted line is the **middle** outcome, not the average one. Weekly receiving yards are lopsided — a receiver priced at 30.5 yards typically gains 24 but *averages* 39, because the big games pull the average up and cannot pull it down. So these projections sit **above** the lines you would see in a betting app, on purpose.

rows.what it means: What the betting markets say this player is worth this week, converted into our scoring. Sportsbooks post a line for his catches, his yards and his chance of scoring; add those up in half-PPR and you get this number.
rows.why it matters: It is the only projection on the page built by people with money at stake, and it already knows about the injury, the weather and the game plan.

rows.what it means: The Vegas number minus our own projection. Positive means the market likes him more than our usage model does; negative means the opposite.
rows.why it matters: The two are built from completely different evidence — one from snaps and targets, one from money. When they disagree by a lot, one of them knows something, and that is worth a look before you set the lineup.

rows.what it means: How many of his scoring categories the sportsbook actually posted a line for. Stars get every market; a backup might only get one.
rows.why it matters: A number built on one market is a thinner read than one built on four.

rows.what it means: True when every scoring category was priced by the book, so the number is entirely the market's. False means we filled a gap — most often the touchdown market — with his own season rate.
rows.why it matters: Trust a FULL row as the market's opinion. Treat the others as mostly the market's, with a patch.
